Subfactors, index and finite-depth classification

Canonical rescaling of Jones cups

A Jones cup can be rescaled inside its actual basic construction so that its expectation onto the upper relative commutant becomes scalar. The resulting projection retains its deeper commutation and implements a faithful normal expectation with the original index. The density formula and its inverse under finite duality give all Jones relations in a prescribed tunnel. In the actual opposite-model commutants, the same rescaled cup implements the trace-preserving basic construction at every depth, including arbitrary centers. An unmarked index-ten pair obstruction distinguishes that construction from original-pair reconstruction; the latter holds at arbitrary depth under the stated extremal strong-amenability hypotheses. The full actual model also has finite bounded bases, trace-preserving center transport two steps apart, and a common atomic center projection. Both opposite centers are atomic or both are diffuse; extremal ordinary cores inherit the same dichotomy without a depth bound.

We use the local-index formula, Theorem2.4; finite common bases, Lesson3; the tracial basic construction and Markov expectation, Lesson4; normal finite expected constructions, Theorem61.2; and the cup functional and representation independence, Lemma62.2. The finite-factor calculations63.1–63.5 use faithful normal representations of finite factors. The opposite-model algebras in63.6–63.8 may have arbitrary centers; their full-corner maps and traces use31.2,43.1 and52.2a, including the complete uniqueness argument52.7j.1–52.7j.4. The abstract-pair comparison63.9–63.10 uses the existing actual PG model, SA.7, CTS.7 and40.1.

Which abstract pair can be reconstructed

Changing the cup in the opposite-model tower does not identify that pair with the original inclusion. In fact the existing index-ten model rules out such an identification even when the comparison map is allowed to be arbitrary.

Theorem 63.9 — an unmarked opposite-pair obstruction. For the actual separable hyperfinite strongly amenable index-ten inclusion of Theorem PG, let be its canonical tracial tower completion. Then

No prescribed finite restriction, cup image or compatibility with the specified reflection is imposed on the forbidden map. Both endpoint algebras of the opposite pair are II₁ factors. Its tracial Jones tower exists by 63.8.

Proof. Keep the actual two-sided interval algebras of PG1–PG14, with left factors , right factors , and physical finite trace. The union of the , , contains every finite interval algebra, so its canonical tracial completion is exactly the actual used there. For every , PG8 and normal expectations onto , , give

Indeed the expectations of a commuting element lie in , converge in tracial , and hence belong to in the limit. Conversely disjoint left and right intervals commute, and their normal closures retain that commutation. PG9 proves that every is a II₁ factor.

Thus the original pair is , and the opposite pair is . Their first relative commutants, with the actual ambient traces, are

The algebra equalities are PG8–PG9; the trace values are the original even- and odd-site weights PG2. These are therefore invariants of the actual limiting inclusions, not only of a finite pair chosen inside them.

An inclusion isomorphism or anti-isomorphism carries the smaller algebra's commutant inside the larger algebra onto the corresponding relative commutant. It also preserves the normalized factor traces. For an abstract von Neumann algebra isomorphism this normality does not need to be added: its positive order isomorphism preserves every bounded increasing supremum, so the map is normal; the same holds for an anti-isomorphism by passage to the opposite algebra. Trace transport and uniqueness of the normalized normal factor trace then give trace preservation. A map between the two displayed algebras must permute their minimal projections. Their weight multisets differ, so no such trace-preserving map exists. This proves (63.36).

The same model already has the actual generating ordinary tunnel and the every-smooth-representation amenability proved in PG3–PG4. Thus none of those hypotheses removes this abstract-pair obstruction. This uses the existing PG model; it is a further invariant consequence of that model, not a second construction.

Corollary 63.10 — arbitrary-depth reconstruction in the extremal case. Let have finite index and separable predual. Assume the original representation amenability: every smooth nondegenerate normal expected representation admits a compatible physical-factor-central state. Assume also ergodicity of the actual ordinary core, as in SA.6–SA.7, and extremality of the inclusion. Then

by a normal trace-preserving map. Finite depth is not required.

Proof. SA.7 constructs an actual generating ordinary tunnel at exactly these strong-amenability and separability hypotheses. Hence its physical standard-part pair is , with the inherited traces. CTS.7 gives equality of the physical and reflected canonical traces at every finite stage under extremality. The normal tracial-extension construction 40.1 therefore extends those compatible finite anti-isomorphisms to the two specified limiting endpoints. In particular reflecting gives , rather than the distinct dual pair . This proves (63.39) at arbitrary depth.

The universal statement in 63.39 cannot omit extremality: Theorem 63.9 meets the other hypotheses and refutes that extension even for arbitrary unmarked maps. This does not make extremality necessary for each individual pair; the different corrected maps in the nonextremal weighted-spin example 62.6 do give an opposite-pair anti-isomorphism there. The tracial opposite tower 63.8, the specified-reflection criterion CTS.7 and the abstract-pair obstruction 63.9 concern three different assertions. None proves a general nonextremal bicommutant or a different represented-core comparison.

Exercise 63.8 — canonical trace and reconstruction. Suppose the algebras in (63.22) have centers. Why does checking the canonical trace only on the full corner still determine its values on the entire positive cone? Does the normal isomorphism (63.34), available separately at every , prove a normal anti-isomorphism from the physical ordinary core to the opposite model?

Solution. Choose an arbitrary maximal family of partial isometries with orthogonal final projections summing to one, as in (52.7j.1). For every positive , any normal trace extending the corner trace has value , with the sum interpreted as the supremum of finite partial sums. Thus equality on the full corner implies equality on every positive element, even with an arbitrary center or an uncountable family; here it gives . In contrast, (63.34) represents each actual opposite-model basic construction on its own tracial Hilbert space. It introduces no anti-isomorphism from the physical core and makes no comparison of the two AF tracial completions. The nonextremal specified-reflection obstruction CTS.7 therefore remains in force, and the separate corrected reconstruction and bicommutant assertions require their own proofs.

Exercise 63.9 — an arbitrary map still preserves root weights. In the index-ten example, can replacing the original cup by the tracial cup of 63.8 remove the obstruction (63.38)? Explain the role of normality, the chosen map and the Jones marking. Contrast the answer with the weighted-spin parameters .

Solution. Changing the cup preserves the actual endpoint algebras and their inherited traces, so the relative commutants and all six trace weights in (63.38) are unchanged. Every abstract pair isomorphism or anti-isomorphism is normal by preservation of increasing positive suprema, and hence preserves the unique normalized factor trace. It must permute the minimal projections of the first relative commutant. The multisets and differ, regardless of the chosen cup or the map's finite restrictions. In the two-label weighted-spin example, the original and opposite weight multisets are both , so this invariant gives no obstruction; the corrected maps in 62.6 actually construct the anti-isomorphism. Equality of that one invariant alone would not prove the existence of such a map for a general model.

Exercise 63.11 — why the second basic construction is needed

In 63.12 explain why the first inequality alone does not prove equality. Locate the dual positive bound and the exact pull-down step that supply the reverse implication.

Solution. The first bound only says that an atomic central corner in has atomic central support in ; it does not exclude atoms of lying over a diffuse part of . Apply the second positive bound to each factor corner . It gives , where is the atomic part of . Full-corner center transport gives , so the positive projection annihilates . The exact formula makes it zero. A statement that adjacent centers are merely abstractly related would not supply this actual equality of projections.

Sources and exact scope

Figure 63.1. The triple and operator mechanisms are proved in 63.1–63.5; positions are schematic. The table uses the actual weighted-spin inclusion in the first worked example and identifies its lower relative commutant with the second site. Its inherited trace, normalized commutant trace and density are distinct columns. The upper first-site relative expectation of the modified cup is scalar, while its expectation onto has the displayed second-site coefficients. Reproducible source.

The human source for the distinction between original and trace-preserving opposite-model cups is Popa, Section1.4.3, printed p.188; the extremal opposite-model comparison is Section1.4.1 and Theorem5.1.1. The full-corner construction and root-weight argument63.6–63.10 are supplied above. The human source for the modified-projection requirement is Sorin Popa, Classification of amenable subfactors of type II, Section4.5.1, printed p.224. The projection construction there is credited to Pimsner and Popa, Entropy and index for subfactors. Propositions63.1 and63.4 and Theorems63.2–63.3 and63.5 give the full finite rescaling proof using Lemma62.2. Popa cites a separate [Po12] comparison for the shifted trace-preserving maps; the cup construction does not supply those maps.

The modified cups63.5 exist in every prescribed tunnel. Theorem63.8 gives their canonical tracial basic-construction interpretation in the actual opposite model, and63.10 gives the original-pair reconstruction at the stated extremal strong-amenability hypotheses. Theorem63.9 refutes the unrestricted nonextremal extension even for arbitrary unmarked pair maps. The whole ordinary-model comparison at arbitrary depth and the extremal physical opposite-model characterization, at their stated hypotheses, are proved in 17.8–17.18. The universal nonextremal inherited-trace pair comparison and the embedded-core assertion have the separate counterexamples 63.9 and 51.7–51.8. The separate unrestricted nonextremal physical bicommutant remains open; the weighted-group case with factorial left balanced completion is proved in PH.29–PH.31.
